acceptedAnswer.text: Find the daily trade count where your own results start to slip, set a trade cap below it before each session, and write down the reason for every trade before placing it. The full protocol: a max loss per trade and per month sized to your tolerance (the two boxes — when the monthly box is empty, the month is over), the hard 3-loss rule, A+ setups only, and scheduled trading windows with the chart closed outside them. Stop trying to fix it with willpower; systems do what intentions can't.

There is no universal number — but the direction of the evidence is clear. In one large trade-tracking dataset's reported analysis of 500,000+ accounts, the share of profitable traders falls from 33.0% among those averaging fewer than 2 trades a day to 15.3% among those averaging 10–15 a day. Your number comes from your own ledger: the count where your results slip, not a guru's. Find it, then cap below it.

mainEntity.name: How many trades per day is too many?

acceptedAnswer.text: Three triggers, almost never a fourth: boredom (the fear of stillness — the trade as entertainment), the post-loss recovery spiral (trading to collect an emotional debt), and overconfidence after a win (the afternoon that forgets the morning's plan). Underneath all three, the same mechanism: the act of placing a trade rewards the brain's dopamine system whether or not the trade makes money.

No — and that's the scary part. Per one large trade-tracking dataset's reported figures, overtrading is detected in 15.4% of accounts under 10 days old but in 70.3% of accounts trading 200+ days; from day 50 onward it's the most common issue traders face. Experience doesn't cure it. It teaches you fancier ways to do it — which is why the protocol above is built for veterans, not beginners.

Five signs: your late-day trades look nothing like your morning ones; you trade because the market is moving rather than because a setup appeared; you're restless in quiet markets; you keep trading after a big win or loss; and your worst results cluster on your highest-trade-count days. The definitive test: tag every trade as strategy or exogenous (outside your plan) in your journal — then compare the two win rates. The gap is your diagnosis.

mainEntity.name: How do I know if I'm overtrading?

acceptedAnswer.text: Revenge trading is one trigger of overtrading — the post-loss recovery circuit. Overtrading also comes from boredom and overconfidence, which revenge trading doesn't cover. The short version: revenge trading is overtrading with a motive; boredom trading is overtrading without one.
